title: The clay, the gold, the iron — know one, know all (6.1)
hook: by knowing one lump of clay, the father says, you know everything made of clay: the pot is only a name

segments.voice: Yesterday: Uddalaka and Shvetaketu, the proud son and the one question. Your line was the one thing worth knowing. Did you ask anyone what they think it is? Day three hundred forty.
screen: `UDDALAKA AND SHVETAKETU — THE ONE THING WORTH KNOWING.`

segments.voice: Look along a kitchen shelf in India and there may well be clay on it. A water pot. A cup for chai, thrown away after one use. A lamp for the evening. A plate, a jar, a tile. Different shapes, different names, different jobs. Shvetaketu has just asked his father how there could possibly be one teaching that makes everything known. And his father doesn't answer with a theory. He points at the pots.
screen: `A POT, A CUP, A LAMP, A JAR.` → `DIFFERENT NAMES, DIFFERENT JOBS.` → `HE POINTS AT THE POTS.`

segments.voice: Uddalaka says: my dear, just as by one lump of clay everything made of clay is known, the change is only a name, a matter of words, and the truth is just clay. In Sanskrit, the end of that line runs: vacarambhanam vikaro namadheyam, mrittiketyeva satyam. The change is a handle of speech, a name; clay alone is the truth. Then he says it twice more. By one gold ornament, everything made of gold is known; the truth is just gold. By one nail-cutter, everything made of iron is known; the truth is just iron. Think about what he's claiming. A pot is real. You can carry water in it. But pot is the name we give to a shape the clay has taken for a while. Break the pot, and nothing has gone out of existence. The clay is still there. It just doesn't answer to pot anymore. So if you understand clay, you understand every pot, every cup, every lamp, all at once, including ones you'll never see. Know the clay, and the names stop confusing you. Now the father is setting up the rest of the chapter. Over the next lessons, the clay will turn out to be something much bigger: what Uddalaka calls Being, the one stuff under every name. Hindu schools have read this line in different ways. Advaita Vedanta, the school of Shankara, hears it as saying the many names are appearance and only the one is ultimately real. Other Vedanta schools, like Ramanuja's, hear the pots as real forms of the one clay. Both schools come back to this lump of clay.
screen: `ONE LUMP OF CLAY.` · `THE CHANGE IS ONLY A NAME.` · `GOLD, AND IRON, THE SAME.` · `TWO SCHOOLS READ THE CLAY.` · then, large: `CLAY ALONE IS THE TRUTH.`

segments.voice: Today's practice looks for the clay. If there's a cup or bowl nearby, hold it, or just picture one. Sit and breathe. Say its name in your mind: cup. Then let the name go and notice what's left: the weight, the coolness, the material. Breathe with that for a while. Then do the same with your own hand. Let the name go. Notice what's there. The bell holds the time.
The clay. Uddalaka's first example: know one lump of clay, and you know all clay; the pot is a name, a matter of words.
Your line: know the clay. Today, when a label gets in the way, a job title, a team, a type of person, try to see the person or the thing under the name. Day three hundred forty.

screen: `DAY 340 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: IN THE BEGINNING, BEING ALONE.`

howItsDone: Vedanta teachers of different schools use Uddalaka's clay, gold and iron as a teaching example, and the clay-and-pot image returns often in later Hindu philosophy.

fork.setup: your son asks how one teaching could make everything known. you have a kitchen full of pots. what do you say?
options: it can't; there's too much to know.
know one lump of clay and you know everything made of clay.
memorize the name of every pot.
fork.reveal: Uddalaka answers with clay, then gold, then iron: the change is only a name; the truth is the material underneath.

original.note: Sanskrit mṛttikā: clay, earth. mṛttikety eva satyam: clay alone is the truth.

trapdoor: what you thought: a lesson about pottery.
what it means: under every name and shape there's one stuff. know it, and the names stop confusing you.
what a scholar hears: vacarambhanam vikaro namadheyam (6.1.4), a key text for Vedanta; Advaita reads the many as appearance, Vishishtadvaita as real modes of one reality.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): hook no longer opens 'Walk into any kitchen' (banned opener and sweeping claim); 'the end of that line is famous' cut; myth reveal 'as the script says' fixed; howItsDone softened.

Gold: 'one gold ornament' (lohamani, sometimes rendered a nugget of gold or copper); iron: 'one nail-cutter' (nakhanikrntana). Confirm renderings; some translators read lohamani as copper.
